321. The aim of the project is to generate resilient livelihoods by increasing the capacity to adapt to climate induced
change in critical upstream and downstream rural communities in Sri Lanka including protection of the ecosystem
service flows that connect them. The project includes activities around land management for irrigation
agriculture, plantations and forest reserves (component 1), promotion of sustainable/green value chains and
payment for ecosystem services (Component 2) and strengthening institutional capacity for land management
(component 3).
322. Main ESMS relevant activities of component 1 include vegetation management to control run-off and enhance
infiltration along roads, rehabilitation of village ponds for water harvesting, climate smart farming techniques for
rice production, increasing efficiency of irrigation, fertilizer and integrated pest control, promoting agroforestry,
home gardens and analog forests through a menu of services including crop diversity, access to germplasm,
nurseries, cultivation practices; restoration and sustainable intensification of plantations through conversion of
under-performing crops into food gardens, agroforestry practices including intercropping with high-value short-
rotation horticultural crops.
323. Under Component 2, the project will strengthen the capacity of farmers and collective groups as enterprises
through advice and training in areas such as agri-processing, product development, branding, certification.
Component 3 is ESMS relevant in the sense that it aims to promote inclusive, multi-stakeholder and evidence-
based land –use planning processes.
 The project is expected to have highly positive environmental impacts as restoration, reforestation and
sustainable land management practices are expected to improve the biodiversity status of the respective
land use systems and improve water infiltration and other ecosystem services. Also, social impacts are
expected to be highly positive as it will improve ecosystem services relevant for local communities including
water, enhance food security and provide other tangible economic benefits for different land owners and
users. However, some risk issues have been identified by the ESMS screening and the details are presented
in Annex A the Screening Report; main issues include:
 Potential need for short-term restrictions on the use of natural resources which might trigger livelihood
impacts;
 Risks that impacts from conservation actions fall disproportionately on disadvantaged or vulnerable
individuals or groups and / or that such groups might be disadvantaged or discriminated with regards to
access to project benefits;
 Potential of insufficient attention to the needs of vulnerable groups when providing alternative livelihood
options or promoting co-management arrangement for land used by communities;
 Introduction of climate proofed tree and crop species might require the use of non-native species with low
risk of developing invasive behavior;
 Potential local environmental impacts related to agri-processing;
 Risks related to a potential use of pesticides when addressing pest infestation triggered by climate change.
 It is not expected that any of the identified risks would likely cause significant adverse environmental and/or
social impacts; most of the risk issues are preliminarily judged as low risk issues, very few as moderate, and
it is expected that they can be readily addressed through good management practices and mitigation
measures. Because priority areas for interventions and further details of project activities will be defined only
during the project’s inception phase, e.g. on the basis of sub-basin planning process, an Environmental and
Social Management Framework (ESMF) has been developed.
 The ESMF delineates the process of assessing risks and identifying suitable mitigation measures, spells out
requirements for consultation and disclosure, establishes implementation arrangements and identifies
financial resources needed for ESMF implementation. It further specifies ESMS relevant socio-economic
data to be gathered by the social baseline analysis carried out during the project inception phase (see topics
identified in the section B and C of the questionnaire). The ESMF also provides detailed guidance for
ensuring compliance with the ESMS Standards. As such it includes elements of an Access Restrictions

=== PAGE 99 ===
F
APPRAISAL SUMMARY
GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL | PAGE 97 OF 124
Mitigation Process Framework (including SIA elements to be included in the social baseline analysis) and
guidance on assessment needs for risk related to the introduction of species and when a Pest Management
Plan will be needed. It also specifies requirements for the project-level grievance mechanisms to be set-up
at project start and which will dovetail with IUCN’s overarching institution-wide ESMS Project Complaints
Management System (PCMS).
324. A Gender Analysis has been carried out that provides an overview of existing gender inequalities in Sri Lanka,
with emphasis on the agricultural and natural resource sectors. It further identifies gender related issues that
are relevant to the proposed project and examines potential gender mainstreaming opportunities to be
implemented by the project. The assessment is based on key available information (listed in the references),
observations made during field visits, and discussions with agriculture and natural resource professional working
in Sri Lanka.
325. The Gender Analysis will be further expanded during the project’s inception phase through in-depth consultations
and focus group discussions to be held in the project site with local communities and other relevant stakeholder
programmed—programmed as an integral part of the social baseline study. The ESMF provides guidance to
ensure that these consultations also serve to capture concerns and assess potential project risks on women and
men.
326. In rural Sri Lanka, women and men have different roles and responsibilities regarding agricultural and natural
resource management. There are tasks that are shared by both genders, those that are dominated by women,
and those that are dominated by men. This results in unique gender-based knowledge, experiences, and
strategies regarding resource management, that are largely unknown to the other gender. To ensure that project
activities achieve maximum success and impact, it is imperative to have equitable involvement, input and
allocation of both women and men in all project interventions. The project will set a target of 35-50% participation
by both genders in all activities. To assure that women have equitable access to project resources, services and
activities the following approach will be applied:
 seek input regarding planning. implementation and priorities from women community leaders and
partners who are respected locally, by government agencies and other partners;
 plan activities to meet women’s time availability, location restrictions, and specific priorities; and
 organize women’s groups and women only activities, if necessary, to provide conditions conducive for
women to participate, share their knowledge and learn more effectively. Experience demonstrates that
this approach will strengthen women’s involvement and knowledge, as well as, enhanced their
confidence regarding their own knowledge of agricultural and natural resource management options,
build their leadership and decision-making capacity, and strengthen their willingness to contribute to
public discussions.
327. Project activities will promote positive social and environmental impacts through the adoption of multi-species
climate-smart agricultural and water management systems, including sloping agricultural land technology and
natural vegetative strips, among poor climate-vulnerable smallholder farmers in both the highlands and the
lowlands. Compared to monocultures, multi-species systems diversify farmers’ livelihoods’ streams, reduce risk
(financial and environmental) and improve biodiversity by incorporating multiple species and varieties on the
same piece of land.
328. A draft Gender Action Plan has been developed which will be further enhanced during the above-mentioned in-
depth consultation with local communities and other relevant stakeholders. The Gender Action Plan provides a
time-bound framework to implement the project’s activities and achieve the project’s outputs, results and
outcomes in an equitable and gender-sensitive manner. It should further contribute to reducing climate change-
induced social, economic and environmental vulnerabilities.

F.4. Financial Management and Procurement
330. The financial management between the AE and EEs of the project will be governed by IUCN’s finance manual
and policy and procedure on procurement of Goods and Services. Further, IUCN comply with Swiss Accounting
Law as well.
331. IUCN has a comprehensive procurement policy in place which is available at
https://portals.iucn.org/union/sites/union/files/doc/procurement_policy_and_procedure_v_1_3_february_2018.p
df. The policy outline formal procurement standards and guidelines across each phase of the procurement
process, and they apply to all procurements in IUCN. The purpose of the policy is to ensure that IUCN obtains
value for money in all its procurement activities and that procurement is conducted in an efficient and cost-
effective manner that respects sustainability, the environment and ethical principles.
332. In addition to the above policies, delegation of authority plays an integral part of the above policies. This policy
mainly outlines the limitation of authority delegated to each category. The policy is available at
https://confluence.iucn.org/display/ERP/IUCN+Policies?preview=%2F589929%2F1605663%2FIUCN_Delegati
on+of+Authority_August2011.pdf
333. IUCN carried out the capacity assessments for all MMDE, ICRAF and IUCN Sri Lanka, the three EES associated
with the GCF investment project and satisfied with the outcome as provided in the letter from IUCN Regional
Director for Asia.
334. Funds will be transferred to IUCN according to the Accreditation Master Agreement (AMA) and the Funded
Activities Agreement (FAA) related to this project. IUCN Headquarters’ Global Finance Unit will manage fund
disbursements to the Project Management Unit based on semi-annual work plans agreed by IUCN supervision
team based in the regional office. Funds will be hosted in a bank account dedicated to the project. PMU is then
responsible for transferring the funds to the executing entities and the services providers or suppliers that would
have been competitively selected. PMU is also responsible to the accounting and fiduciary management of all
funds disbursed. The PMU will adopt IUCN’s accounting systems and will be audited independently (auditors
selected through a competitive bidding process where TORs are approved by IUCN Global Finance Unit) on a
yearly basis.

G.1. Risk Assessment Summary
The main environmental and social risk factors are:
 Potential need for short-term restrictions on the use of natural resources which might trigger livelihood
impacts;
 Social risks related to potentially perceived unfair treatment or discrimination with regards to access to
project benefits;
 Potential of insufficient attention to the needs of vulnerable groups when providing alternative livelihood
options or promoting co-management arrangement for land used by communities;
 Introduction of climate proofed tree and crop species might require the use of non-native species with
low risk of developing invasive behavior;
 Potential local environmental impacts related to agri-processing;
 Risks related to a potential use of pesticides when addressing pest infestation triggered by climate
change.
Technical/operational and financial risk factors are:
 Conflict between communities and governments or levels of government (local, provincial, and national)
over land use and natural resource planning may hamper implementation. Instability, conflict, and/or
tensions may then constrain project implementation.
 Stakeholders adopt patterns of corruption, collusion and nepotism, endangering the introduction of good
governance practices.
 A ‘project’ mentality develops where local people expect monetary compensation to participate in
activities. A similar mentality may develop with government or other partners.
 Partners maybe unwilling or unable to follow project planning and/or project reporting protocols.
G.2. Risk Factors and Mitigation Measures
Selected Risk Factor 1
Probability of risk

Mitigation Measure(s)
Reforestation of degraded lands in catchment areas might require restricting the access to those areas which are used
by local communities for cattle grazing, firewood and other needs but is driving deforestation, until the vegetation is
stable. It will only be during project implementation that the need of such restrictions is decided. The Environmental
and Social Management Framework (ESMF) which includes relevant provisions from the Standard on Involuntary
Resettlement and Access Restrictions (elements of a Process Framework) provide guidance on assessing the risk on
local communities and developing suitable mitigation measures to be agreed with project affected people or
communities. One mitigation measure already pre-identified is to put these restoration areas under a form of co-
management (shared management between communities and the respective government agency) hence sharing not
only decision making between those actors but also future benefits of resource harvesting. This and the application
of the Standard’s requirements are expected to reduce the probability of the risk occurring to low.

Mitigation Measure(s)
The project will adopt an inclusive and participatory planning approach when planning the details of project activities
based on the stakeholder engagement strategy. Where beneficiaries of support activities (e.g. training on agricultural
practices, business services such as certification, quality assurance, processing and collective marketing) need to be
selected, this will be done in a transparent way with clear eligibility criteria to increase transparency and avoid
unintended discrimination. For some activities the project will use a ‘first ready, first served’ approach to identify
beneficiaries who are best prepared to succeed; while at the same time assisting new or less developed groups to
become ‘ready’ to fully engage in project activities. Allocation of benefits might further follow the need to provide
assistance or compensation to people affected by access restrictions (see risk factor 1). The executing entities will
also use ‘farmer-to-farmer’ exchange to build partnership and healthy competition.
The project-level grievance mechanism is expected to further minimize tensions or conflicts building up applying a
proactive approach to grievance and maintaining a constructive relationship with stakeholders to identify and anticipate
potential issues early. These mitigation measures will reduce the probability of the risk occurring to low.

Mitigation Measure(s)
The project will not fund the actual application of pesticides or chemicals and mostly work on the awareness and
education side of pesticide use. E.g. promotion of weed control through simple mechanical hand weeders instead
herbicides and of integrated pest control based on real time weather and pest incidence data. These activities are
expected to lead to a reduction of quantities of biocide applied by farmers and plantations. Nevertheless, as climate
change increase the prevalence of pests, there might be a situation where advisory services funded by the project
might need to advice on targeted application of pesticides. The adherence to the IUCN Guidance Note on Pest
Management Planning as described in the ESMF will further reduce the low probability of the risk occurring.

Other Potential Risks in the Horizon
Risks that may emerge and need to be monitored, include:
 Project implementation may strain the capacity and resources of local government agencies.
 Due to limited availability of local expertise, it may prove difficult to access qualified staff to effectively
implement the project.
 The procurement of the supplies and materials required to implement activities and support partners may be
difficult or expensive to procure, thus hampering project implementation
 Traders and other private sector stakeholders may be reluctant to work with farmers in an equitable and
transparent fashion.
 Off-farm income generating opportunities may reduce farmers’ investment in management options promoted
by the project, hampering activities under all three outcomes.

Paradigm shift objectives
The project catalyzes a paradigm shift in Subsistence Farmers and Agricultural Plantation
Communities residing in the vulnerable river basins, watershed areas and downstream of the
Increased climate- Knuckles Mountain Range Catchment of Sri Lanka can sustain income and food security levels
resilient sustainable because they have the information, services including finance & investments and skills they need
development to successfully adapt land and water management and agricultural practices to changes in
temperatures and rainfall.

47 Direct beneficiaries are those who come into direct contact with the set of interventions (goods or services) provided by the
investment. Individuals who receive training or benefit from program-supported technical assistance or service provision are considered
direct beneficiaries. Services include training and technical assistance provided directly by program staff, and training and technical
assistance provided by people who have been trained by program staff. If cooperatives or organizations receive training or technical
assistance from the program, all members of the cooperative/organization are considered direct beneficiaries.
Indirect beneficiaries are those who benefit indirectly from the goods and services provided to the direct beneficiaries (as defined
above). For example, indirect beneficiaries include members of the household of a beneficiary farmer who received technical assistance,
seeds, tools, inputs, credit, livestock; farmers from a neighbouring community who might observe the effects of the training and
demonstration plots in the target community and decide to adopt or model the new practices themselves; the population of all of the
communities in a valley that uses a road improved by a food for work activity; or all individuals who may have heard a radio message

57 The project will track uptake and usage of tools, instruments, strategies and activities developed by the project. Numbers reported
are a use intensity index (UII) where the UII = (sumN ((1/((Nh - Nhu)/Nh)) * (1/((F - Fu)/Fu)) / Nt) x100; where: sumN is the sum across
all project tools, instruments etc., Nh is total number of vulnerable households, Nhu is number of vulnerable households using the tool, F
is the maximum desirable mean frequency of use; Fu the actual mean frequency of use and Nt the number of tools. Separate in depth
survey for each tool will be conducted to track respondent feedback on impact of use on their response to climate variability.

Analog forests model the process of natural
forest development and forest service
functions in (re)establishing a sustainable
ecosystem characterized by a high
biodiversity to biomass ratio. Analog forests
are designed through a synthesis of
traditional and scientific knowledge, to
optimize the production and service
potential of the system rather than to
maximize the productivity of a single
species component. While focused on
ecosystem restoration, analog forests are
also designed to provide economic
benefits. Annual species are also
components of analog forests.
Home gardens, spice gardens, annual
horticultural systems, and analog forests
can be viewed as a continuum of
smallholder systems. From horticultural
systems focused on annual crops, to home
gardens and spice gardens representing
perennial (tree) farming systems, to analog
forests being a forest management and
restoration approach. All include both
annual and perennial species and are
concerned with sustainable management.

spice gardens and annual horticultural
systems focus on enhancing smallholder
livelihoods in an environmentally
sustainable manner; and analog forests

H.2. Arrangements for Monitoring, Reporting and Evaluation
331. Project level monitoring and evaluation will be undertaken in compliance with the IUCN 2015
Monitoring and Evaluation Policy, Accreditation Master Agreement (AMA) between GCF and
IUCN and the IUCN Access to Information Policy.
332. Project monitoring will measure achievement of the performance indicators and report on the
implementation progress of GCF project while it is being implemented. Performance indicators
are identified according to the principles established in the GCF Initial Results Management
Framework linking Time-bound sets of activities to a set of agreed adaptation results. IUCN
maintains a standard list of technically well-informed indicators aligned to its donors core
indicators, including GCF. IUCN aims to develop its standard indicators for each programmatic
area with afferent measurement tools to ensure effective data collection and harmonized
reporting. IUCN’s Programme and Project Portal allows efficient and timely data management and
project information disclosure
333. A project inception workshop will be held after the project document is signed by all relevant
parties to: a) re-orient project stakeholders to the project strategy and discuss any changes in the
overall context that influence project implementation; b) discuss the roles and responsibilities of
the project team, including reporting and communication lines and conflict resolution mechanisms;
c) review the results framework, re-assess baselines as needed, and discuss reporting, monitoring
and evaluation roles and responsibilities and finalize the M&E plan; d) review financial reporting
procedures and mandatory requirements, and agree on the arrangements for the annual audit; e)
plan and schedule Project Board meetings and finalize the first year annual work plan. IUCN will
prepare the inception report no later than one month after the inception workshop. The final
inception report will be cleared by the National Steering Committee before submission to the GCF
Secretariat.
334. A Project Implementation Report (PIR) will be prepared for each year of project implementation.
Each report is cleared by the National Steering Committee before submission to the GCF
Secretariat. The Programme Director of the project, the IUCN Country Office, and the IUCN
Regional Technical Advisor will provide objective input to the annual PIR. The Programme Director
will ensure that the indicators included in the project results framework are monitored annually
well in advance of the implementation report submission deadline and will objectively report
progress. The annual implementation report will be shared with the National Steering Committee
and other stakeholders. IUCN will coordinate the input of the NDA Focal Point and other
stakeholders to the implementation report. The final project implementation report, along with the
terminal evaluation report, will serve as the final project report package.
335. Project mid-term (MTE) and final (FE) evaluations will be commissioned and managed by the
IUCN Planning, Monitoring, Evaluation and Risk Unit – IUCN’s independent evaluation office.
Independent evaluators under the oversight of PMER will be contracted to conduct these
evaluations. The evaluation criteria are aligned to the GCF IEU Evaluation Criteria. The MTE will
assess (1) the relevance, effectiveness, efficiency and likelihood of impact and sustainability, (2)
the coherence in climate finance delivery, (3) gender equity and social inclusion (minorities), (3)
and country ownership. The FE will assess (1) the relevance, effectiveness, efficiency and
likelihood of impact and sustainability, (2) the coherence in climate finance delivery, (3) gender
equity and social inclusion (minorities), (3) and country ownership, (4) innovativeness in result
areas, and (6) replication and scalability. The evaluation will apply a process tracing methodology.
Data collection will include stakeholder interviews, site visits and documentary reviews. The IUCN
management response will be reviewed by the National Steering Committee. Evaluation reports

337. In addition to the above, National Steering Committee will be gathered quarterly or more often
than that as per the requirement and monitor the progress against the annual project
implementation plan. The Executive Entities which are IUCN, Ministry of Mahaweli Development
and Environment and ICRAF will be responsible to lead the presentations of the progress for the
out puts and activities they are responsible. Under the facilitation of the EE the contracted
organizations for each sub activities (that are in line with the project TOC and the budget) will be
presented the progress. Any bottlenecks will be exposed at this forum and the National Steering
Committee will provide or get immediate actions to the internally and externally popped up issues.

II. Summary of the Secretariat’s assessment
2.1 Project background
3. The “Strengthening climate resilience of subsistence farmers and agricultural plantation
communities residing in the vulnerable river basins, watershed areas and downstream of the
Knuckles Mountain Range catchment of Sri Lanka” project aims to strengthen the adaptive

Assessment Methodology, the System of Rice Intensification, and the Payment for Ecosystem Services Mechanism.

=== PAGE 134 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 134
capacity of smallholder subsistence farmers to address climate-induced irrigation and drinking
water shortages by improving the resilience of farm- and land-management practices, and by
climate proofing the underlying ecosystems in the Knuckles/Amban Ganga highlands and
lowlands. The interventions are focused on:
(a) Promoting sustainable land use and profitability of farming and plantation management
in upstream areas, as well as the efficient use of irrigation water and climate-adapted
agriculture downstream;
(b) Implementing sustainable financing to enable investment in catchment protection and
sustainable land use through value-chain upgrading and the establishment of payment
for ecosystem service schemes, respectively; and
(c) Providing institutional support to develop appropriate governance mechanisms,
information systems and rural advisory services capable of delivering appropriate land
use options across the project area.
4. The project area covers the upper watershed and downstream areas of the Knuckles
Mountain Range, which is a United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
Heritage Site that includes key biodiversity hotspots and forest reserves. The region is
dominated by tea plantations and forests (natural and plantation) along with other field crops
and home gardens. The water absorbed and released is used for power generation, agriculture
within the mountain and downstream areas, and domestic consumption. The reservoirs in the
upstream catchment are the primary source of irrigation water for agriculture and other
livelihoods in the downstream command area comprising 506,260 ha, of which 122,150 ha are
covered in irrigated rice.
5. Increases in temperature and windspeed as well as a shift in the intensity of seasonal
rainfall are observed to accelerate the intensity and frequency of extreme events, such as floods,
landslides and droughts that are erosive. Increased erosion and sedimentation in the upstream
catchments reduce the reservoir capacity as well as soil quality, in turn, increasing food
insecurity for smallholder and subsistence farmers in the downstream area where irrigation
supply is inadequate for agricultural practices.
6. The total project finance needed is USD 48.975 million, with a request to GCF for grant
finance of USD 39.775 million (81 per cent). The Ministry of Mahaweli Development and
Environment (MMDE) is contributing USD 5.9 million in the form of grants, in addition to USD 3
million and USD 0.3 million in the form of grants contributed through the Mahaweli Authority of
Sri Lanka and Forest Department, respectively.
2.2 Component-by-component analysis
Component 1: Climate‐resilient sustainable land management (total cost: USD 21.72 million; GCF
cost: USD 16.74 million)
7. This component aims to improve land and water management with two key outputs:
(a) Safeguarding the production of environmental goods and services in the upstream
catchment area: the interventions to achieve this output will build on providing relevant
information on climate change, land and water management practices to farmers and
other land users in the upstream catchment area as well as reducing sedimentation that
decreases water availability for downstream irrigation; and
(b) Increasing the productivity and climate resilience of primary production in both
upstream catchment and downstream irrigated agricultural areas: this will be achieved
through supporting the local stakeholders and land users, including farmers, foresters

=== PAGE 135 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 135
and plantation companies/workers, to adopt efficient water-use and irrigation
techniques.
8. The proposed interventions under this component take an integrated approach, where
the downstream catchment area is to benefit through interventions in the upstream catchment
area, by ensuring a continuum between upstream and downstream hydrological and ecosystem
benefits.
Component 2: Secure financing mechanisms for sustainable land management (total cost: USD
12.96 million; GCF cost: USD 10.46 million)
9. This component focuses on sustaining improved land management through the
establishment of sustainable financing. Interventions under this component include upgrading
green value chains with increased efficiency and linkages to new markets and establishing a
payment for ecosystem services (PES) mechanism.
10. The proposed interventions are expected to enhance the sustainable outcomes of
interventions under component 1 by establishing systems that create business cases and ensure
profitability of sustainable land use and farming. Detailed mapping of agricultural value chains
and regular market analysis will be conducted to provide the basis for value-chain upgrading
options for the smallholder and subsistence farmers in the upstream catchment area. Through
the establishment of value-chain innovation platforms, the project will set up “soft” institutions
where needed, such as cooperatives; innovation platforms; producer, agri-business and trade
associations; or chambers of commerce overseas.
11. Building upon lessons learned from other Asian countries, the establishment of a PES
mechanism is expected to provide financial incentives for the continuance of climate adaptive
catchment protection practices. It will involve establishing an adaptive rural advisory service
facility to provide technical support through sharing knowledge and real-time information on
climate risks as well as best-fit options for the local context. A series of capacity strengthening
activities will be conducted for local stakeholders to strengthen their capacity to monitor,
evaluate and develop further relevant criteria and indicators, when there is a need to modify
existing, or establish new, PES schemes in the future.
Component 3: Strengthen institutional capacity (total cost: USD 12.23 million; GCF cost: USD 10.98
million)
12. This component aims to address the existing constraints in governance structure as well
as the hydrological boundaries. Interventions will promote an integrated governance
mechanism through increased coordination of expertise across different ministries and
departments to support the development of land use policy, planning and intervention options
at the subbasin level. Multi-stakeholder innovation platforms, set up at the subbasin level, will
facilitate such horizontal as well as vertical integration.
13. Under this component, the project aims to improve land use policy and planning with
increased understanding of the local context, through multi-stakeholder consultations.
Information will be shared through online dashboards developed to support the identification
and implementation of appropriate adaptive options in sustainable land use and management.
To this end, training guides, guidelines and tools will be developed.
Project management (total cost: USD 2.1 million; GCF cost: USD 1.6 million)
14. GCF grant financing represents 77 per cent of the total project management costs. The
requested project management costs amount to 4.19 per cent of the total grant requested from
GCF.

GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 136
III. Assessment of performance against investment criteria
3.1 Impact potential Scale: Medium‐High
15. The proposed project has multiple impacts at the project sites and important additional
benefits downstream of the project area. In the project area, current unsustainable land use
practices will be made climate resilient through improved land use planning and management
and the introduction of land use practices that are more responsive to climate change. Past
management practices favoured the clearing of trees on agricultural lands and mono-cropping
of annual crops, leading to severe land degradation and erosion, and siltation in reservoirs
below the highlands. The project will introduce improved land use practices, based on
indigenous perennials, leading to a reversal of land degradation, a reduction in erosion and
siltation in downstream reservoirs, and an increased streamflow for a longer period throughout
the year, which will support irrigated cropping in the lowlands.
16. The project will build institutional capacity in sustainable land management in
government agencies at local and national levels. This increased capacity will lead to sustained
support for sustainable land management after the closure of the project.
3.2 Paradigm shift potential Scale: High
17. The project area is characterized by large commercial estates – mostly tea plantations –
and small-scale farms that produce annual crops. Both the estates and the farms employ land
use practices that are geared towards mechanization (removal of trees, upscaling), even though
the geography of the area is not amenable to such practices and it increases vulnerability to
climate change. The project will introduce a form of productive land use based on the local
ecosystem potential, reintroducing native trees and other perennials. This system of perennial
land cover leads to increased resilience to climate change through an improved capture of
precipitation (reduced storm run-off) and a more diverse production system that reduces the
risk of catastrophic crop failure.
18. The project will build institutional capacity to support this model of so-called analogue
forestry in government agencies at local and national levels. Given that the approach is based
principally on local ecosystem properties and capacities, upscaling to other areas in Sri Lanka,
with the increased capacity in, for instance, extension services, is relatively straightforward.
19. The increased and improved streamflow – larger volume of streamflow, over a longer
period into the dry season, with a lower sediment load – benefits the downstream users in the
Mahaweli irrigation system. A PES scheme will be established through which the reservoir
operators transfer funds to the land users in the project area that are demonstrably managing
their land in a way that benefits downstream water users. This would be the first PES scheme at
scale undertaken in Sri Lanka.
3.3 Sustainable development potential Scale: High
20. The project will introduce analogue forestry as an integrated land use system revolving
around indigenous tree species assemblages, reaching maximum ecosystem productivity
yielding a variety of commercially interesting crops, such as vegetables, fruits, herbs, tubers,
medicinal plants and mushrooms. These are important co-benefits for the participating
smallholder farmers, as the economic return on these crops is better than the current annual
crops and the exposure to catastrophic crop loss due to climate variability or pests (which may
themselves be driven by climate change) is much reduced through the production of multiple
crops.

=== PAGE 137 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 137
21. The project introduces a PES scheme that makes a sustainable flow of financial
resources available to the project beneficiaries in the project area.
3.4 Needs of the recipient Scale: Medium
22. Sri Lanka has experienced a remarkable economic development since the end of its civil
war. Gross domestic product has grown exponentially, and poverty levels have dropped in line
with this. That notwithstanding, Sri Lanka has limited fiscal space to undertake projects of this
kind due to a high level of indebtedness.
23. Sri Lanka is experiencing significant impacts from climate change, specifically through
changing precipitation patterns. The main agricultural production areas are highly dependent
on a stable supply on irrigation water, which this project is helping to supply.
3.5 Country ownership Scale: High
24. The funding proposal aligns with all the national policies on climate change and the
nationally determined contribution submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on
Climate Change secretariat. During a country visit of the GCF Secretariat to Sri Lanka, the
delegation was received by the President of Sri Lanka, also acting as Minister of Environment;
the President stressed the importance of the sustainable management of the central highlands
as an ecological cornerstone for all other areas of the island.
25. The funding proposal was developed largely with national counterparts – the main
intervention of analogue forestry was developed by an internationally recognized Sri Lankan
academic.
3.6 Efficiency and effectiveness Scale: Medium‐High
26. The project requires a substantial investment in the form of grants, but there are many
beneficiaries, including in downstream project areas. The overall cost-effectiveness of the
project is demonstrated by an economic internal rate of return (EIRR) of 21 per cent over 20
years. The benefit streams result from the reduced costs as a result of erosion and sediment;
increased income from higher crop intensity; increased household income from better quality
and marketing of products, community forestry and tourism; and reduced compensation due to
fewer disasters. However, these calculations still need to be verified when the Secretariat
receives the detailed economic model. The mitigation benefit calculated over the total project
budget is USD 25.30/tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent.
27. The level of concessionality can be partially justified by market failures and the
provision of public goods. Output 2.2, the establishment of a PES scheme, provides a continuous
source of finance for the project area, which is considered to be an important benefit to
safeguard the investment. This output directly addresses a market failure, and outputs 1.1, 3.1
and 3.2 have characteristics of public good. Outputs 1.2 and 2.1 concern private enterprise
development, although the accredited entity (AE) has argued that this development is essential
to produce the public good of preserving the upstream catchment. Further review of the
economic model will be necessary to see if the value of these instances of public good justify the
requested grant element for these activities.
IV. Assessment of consistency with GCF safeguards and policies
4.1 Environmental and social safeguards

=== PAGE 138 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 138
28. The AE has completed a screening procedure and classified the project as having
moderate risk. The Secretariat confirms this is equivalent to GCF’s environmental and social risk
category B. The project aims to generate resilient livelihoods by increasing the adaptive capacity
to climate induced changes in critical upstream and downstream rural communities of the
Knuckles mountain range areas in Sri Lanka. The activities are focused towards land
management for irrigation agriculture, plantations and forest reserves; promotion of
sustainable and green value chains; payment for ecosystem services; and strengthening
institutional capacity for land management.
29. The AE has developed an environmental and social management framework (ESMF)
that provides a platform for the development and operation stages of the project to effectively
and efficiently manage environmental and social issues and concerns. An ESMF has been
developed as the specific sites that have to be identified and developed in detail together with
the relevant local-level stakeholders will only be decided during the project implementation
stage. The ESMF has described the environmental and social context of the area, including water
resources, soil and forest areas. It has described the socio-economic context, including
population, ethnic distribution, income and educational demographics. The ESMF was disclosed
in English and a Non-Technical Summary was disclosed in Sinhala and Tamil languages.
30. The ESMF provided provided an analysis of the relevant national policy and regulatory
framework in the country and identified measures to ensure project’s compliance with the AE’s
and GCF environmental and social safeguards. It also identified potential environmental and
social risk and impacts based on the proposed activities. Among these include the potential for
erosion and sediment movement during streamside protection and drainage management along
roads especially if done during the rainy season. The rehabilitation and establishment of village
tanks, ponds and irrigation networks could also lead to loss of vegetation and top-soil causing
erosion as well as expose the community members to possible accidents and water-borne and
water-related diseases. The increase in cropping intensity might also lead to decrease in surface
water quality through increased use of fertilizers and pesticides. The possible environmental
and social risks and impacts that are identified have been provided with mitigation measures
through a preliminary risk management plan. While landscape forest restoration interventions
could lead to temporary restrictions to access and use of forest land and resources, the ESMF
provided for a mechanism whereby decisions are taken voluntarily by those who are
collectively using the area and resources for their livelihood. An action plan to mitigate the
impacts from access restrictions will be developed should access restrictions be considered
necessary.
31. The ESMF included procedures for identifying and managing environmental and social
risks of sub-projects. This comprises having a criteria that will guide in the site selection,
reference to an exclusion list that describes the sub-projects that are considered high risk
projects and would not be supported, a screening procedure, a due diligence procedure
including impact assessment particularly for moderate risk sub-projects and clearance for low
risk sub-projects, and development and implementation of mitigation measures through an
environmental and social management plan including its monitoring and supervision. The AE
undertook screening to determine the presence of indigenous peoples, particularly Vedda
people, and found that there is no presence of Vedda people in the project's area of influence.
Additional examination is planned during the social baseline study and associated community
consultations to analyze the presence of any ethnic groups present in the sites that meet both
the AE and GCF's broader definition of indigenous peoples. The examination will take into
account the impacts to communities of any restrictions planned as part of the reforestation
process and ensure that alternatives are provided.
32. The AE will delegate an ESMS officer who will be responsible for the overall supervision
of the ESMF implementation in accordance to the AE’s role as implementing and supervising
agency. It will be complemented by the project team/Project Management Unit (PMU) hosted at

=== PAGE 139 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 139
the AE’s country office. The executing entities will be responsible for the implementation of the
respective sub-projects as well as in implementing the mitigation measures at the site level. A
safeguards training on the ESMF for all project staff and relevant project partners are planned to
be conducted during the inception phase of the project. An indicative budget for implementing
the ESMF is also provided.
33. Stakeholder consultations with government agencies, civil society organizations and
communities were undertaken throughout the project design process. Provisions for continued
stakeholder engagement and information disclosure are described in the project’s stakeholder
engagement plan. The ESMF also specifies requirements for the project-level grievance
mechanisms to be set up at the start of the project and that will complement the project
complaints management system of the AE.
4.2 Gender policy
34. The proposal contains a gender assessment and gender action plan; therefore, it
complies with the GCF Gender Policy and Gender Action Plan. The assessment provides
information on the enabling environment in Sri Lanka to promote gender equality and women’s
empowerment; voting and education rights being well-established in the country. The national
policy and legal framework for promoting gender equality in Sri Lanka includes a women’s
rights bill and international instruments for assuring women's rights, which have been ratified
though both need either approval or incorporation into national legislation. Sri Lanka has also
established the Ministry of Women and Child Affairs, and a policy on women has been drafted.
The gender assessment describes the gender issues at a national level in terms of access to
healthcare, education, participation in the labour market (which for women generally offers
limited economic opportunities due to low paying jobs in laborious industries, agriculture and
informal sectors), and low participation in political decision-making for women. Discrimination
against women is also prevalent in the areas of inheritance and property rights given the
patriarchal nature of cultural norms and beliefs, which in turn, holding women and girls back
from getting equal opportunities and benefits from overall development.
35. The gender assessment also provides an analysis of gender issues in agriculture, natural
resource management, and small and medium enterprises (SMEs). The assessment indicates
that there are designated roles and responsibilities for women and men, in irrigated rice,
horticulture and home gardens, while it indicates concerns in the livestock, plantations and
forest and natural resource management. In the later activities, it indicates that women have
more influence over home gardens given that produce is mainly used at the household level.
However, women seem to have less access to capital, inputs, extension services and market
information for agricultural purposes, while are paid lower wages when working as laborers in
plantations. Regarding activities related to forests, men are involved in timber harvesting and
collection of other high-value forest products while women collect non-timber forest products
for household use. Though both women and men can be in forest management committees,
women play a greater role in monitoring, and they also participate in forest rehabilitation
works. However, the assessment indicates that women are unseen contributors to forest
protection and therefore, in fact, have limited direct power in forest protection activities. In
relations to SMEs, women face challenges such as lack of access to finance, financial literacy,
negative norms and practices, limited mobility and unequal share in household responsibilities.
The assessment also articulates the vulnerabilities women face as a result of climate change, for
example, diminished access to water in drier conditions. The design of the project has
mainstreamed gender issues across the various components. The mainstreamed activities have
considered interventions which build on women’s already existing capacities and knowledge as
well as increasing opportunities for women to engage in other important forestry and
agricultural related activities that will have returns to development of themselves, communities
and families. An additional and important expected benefit that the assessment points out is the

=== PAGE 140 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 140
positive nutritional returns to women’s enhanced engagement. The assessment clearly
demonstrates these considerations.
36. The proposal contains a Gender Action Plan outlining activities and tentative indicators
with sex-disaggregated targets that are aligned with the project components. The Gender Action
Plan is aligned with the logic framework in setting disaggregated targets. The action plan
includes many activities that are aimed at addressing various challenges that women are
expected to face in effectively engaging in the project. These activities include, but are not
limited to, the followings: opportunities for women to engage in paid-labours; active
engagement of women in the design, development and management of farmers’ woodlots;
engagement in water quality measurement and monitoring of the irrigation water use
efficiency; opportunities for women to increase income through commercialization of their
production; allocation of underutilized land to women, including female-headed households;
development of women’s entrepreneurial skills on identification of market opportunities
product development and marketing; skills and knowledge development for women in tourism
sector; and enhanced opportunities through the Green Listing process. The action plan also
includes capacity development initiatives targeted at various groups on mainstreaming gender,
developments of tools and collection of sex disaggregated data.
37. The Gender Action Plan is however expected to be fine-tuned following identification of
the sites for the intervention and completion of the rapid social analysis and in-depth
consultations with stakeholders. The AE will ensure that the social baseline analysis and
collection of data are conducted prior to commencing implementation of the project. The
baseline, targets, indicators and timelines are therefore also expected to be refined as needed
for all the activities, and those that are already included are to be updated based on the findings.
The PMU and the gender specialist that will be hired will be responsible for the implementation
of the Gender Action Plan. Budget has been allocated for the implementation of the Gender
Action Plan.
4.3 Risks
4.3.1. Overall programme assessment (medium risk)
38. The funding proposal requests a GCF grant of USD 39.7 million, accounting for 79 per
cent of the total financing. The total project cost is USD 48.9 million with co-financing by way of
grants from the government entities of Sri Lanka. There is no co-financing from the AE.
39. There are three executing entities (EEs) namely, the International Union for
Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Sri Lanka Country Office, MMDE and the International Centre for
Research in Agroforestry (ICRAF). All three components involve two EEs and five out of six
outputs will be implemented by two EEs. While the AE has described project activities, some
specifics will be finalized during the implementation. This may impact the livelihood of the
beneficiaries. For instance, the project may need potential short-term restrictions on the use of
natural resources; and specific intervention locations for ground activities have yet to be
finalized. These can only be determined during project implementation according to the AE. The
success of the project implementation depends on efficient coordination among the AE, EEs and
other relevant stakeholders to ensure transparency and equity with respect to access to the
project benefit.
4.3.2. Accredited entity/executing entity capability to execute the current programme
(medium risk)
40. IUCN has operated in Sri Lanka for over 20 years and has worked with the country’s
government. The IUCN Asia Regional office and IUCN Headquarters will be responsible for

=== PAGE 141 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 141
oversight of the project and ensuring its progress. The IUCN Sri Lanka Country Office will play
the role of EE.
41. The three EEs have a track record in project implementation. The MMDE is a national
designated authority and the project management unit (PMU) will be established in the
ministry. IUCN Sri Lanka will provide technical services and manage most of the activities based
on its experience and expertise. ICRAF will provide technical advice for components 2 and 3.
The AE carried out the assessment of the procurement and financial capacity of MMDE and
ICRAF and confirmed that the EEs have the required capacities, experience and policies.
4.3.3. Programme‐specific execution risks (medium risk)
42. Finalization of specific locations for interventions: the funding proposal aims to support
a rainwater harvesting infrastructure (activity 1.1.2) and irrigation system for agriculture
(activity 1.2.1). It is estimated that 1,084 villages will benefit from these activities. However, the
specific locations for interventions at the ground level will be finalized during the
implementation after consultation with communities.
43. Conflicts among stakeholders and discrimination against certain groups: the funding
proposal outlined as risks potential conflicts among stakeholders and discrimination against
certain groups over project benefit sharing, access to project resources and land use planning at
community and government levels. Other risks are related to corruption, collusion and
nepotism, and endangering the good governance practices as identified by the AE. The AE
suggested multiple mitigants, such as setting up clear eligibility criteria, creating a multi-
stakeholder platform, engaging in continuous consultation, and the promotion of transparent
and participatory practices. It will also focus on areas where communities have a history of
collaboration and conflict resolution for its initial project implementation. Given that specific
locations for interventions still to be finalized as mentioned above, the AE and EEs are relied
upon to execute mitigants and monitor such risks during the project implementation.
44. Potential restriction on the use of natural resources: the AE identified a potential need
for short-term restrictions on the use of natural resources as a risk because it might affect the
livelihood of the local communities. It can be only determined during the project
implementation. The AE already identified mitigants through the Standard on Involuntary
Resettlement and Access Restrictions as well as a shared management mechanism between
communities and the respective government agency.
45. Economic viability: section F.1 of the funding proposal includes the economic analysis
with a number of assumptions and five independent benefit streams identified based on the
results framework to compute the values. The analysis yielded an EIRR of 21 per cent based on
benefits estimated by AE and lifespan of benefits over 20 years under the base case scenario.
Sensitivity analysis was undertaken, and the worst-case scenario assumed a 10 per cent
increase in cost and a 10 per cent reduction in benefit at the same time, which resulted in the
EIRR of 15 per cent.
4.3.4. Compliance risk (medium risk)
46. This is a project addressing water needs in the subject territorial area. In response to
inquiries from the compliance team regarding potential risks that would make the project
vulnerable to money-laundering, terrorist financing or prohibited practices, the AE responded
that the project will have several safeguards in place to counteract these potential risks and
threats.
47. The overall governance structure of the project will be provided by the government’s
MMDE through the Project Board with the Secretary of MMDE, who is also the Chief Accounting
Officer chairing the Project Board (or the National Steering Committee (NSC)). The project will

be subject to AE oversight, with audits being conducted for each EE. The AE has reviewed the

will impact the water availability for land use improvements, including new plantings. Sri
Lanka’s disaster response capacity is significant and, therefore, disasters will not disturb the
project much. Having reviewed the project proposal and the AE assessment of risk and
mitigation measures, Compliance assigns this project with a medium rating.

4.5 Results monitoring and reporting
57. This is a project that seeks transformation at ambitious scales, building on approaches,
tools, capacities and a political will that reduce risk of failure. The project aims to support the
communities to improve the efficiency of water, land and energy uses, and engage in value-
added products, minimizing pre-harvest waste, such as fertilizer and water and post-harvest
losses. While doing so, the sustainability of the project is ensured by applying the PES
approaches to maintain infrastructure, such as stream banks and roads, etc., and benefits to the
community through value-added agriculture and tourism, allowing them to better understand
the value of ecosystems for quality livelihoods while meeting the climate challenges.
58. It is an adaptation project that is meant to protect 411,564 ha of upland and lowland
agro-systems. The project is also estimated to have the capacity to sequester 1.9 million tCO eq
2
over a period of six years from improved forest management and land use. The project is
expected to impact an anticipated 1.074 million (100 per cent) beneficiaries (51.3 per cent
female and 48.7 per cent male), including 268,643 direct beneficiaries (138,003 female and
130,640 female) located in the intervention area. Indirect beneficiaries of the project are
estimated at 522,561 males and 552,012 females.
59. The project will contribute to achieving three fund-level impacts, namely:
(a) Increased resilience and enhanced livelihoods for the most vulnerable people,
communities and regions;
(b) Increased resilience of health and well-being, and food and water security; and
(c) improved resilience of ecosystems and ecosystem services.
60. Regarding the theory of change diagram, this shows a clear causal linkage between the
barriers and proposed intervention with clear reference to assumptions and risks.
61. Regarding the timetable of implementation, earlier comments have been addressed and
the project now conforms with the standard GCF format.
62. For the logical framework, the revised funding proposal incorporated most of the
comments and suggestions provided by the Secretariat and already conforms with GCF
performance measurement frameworks and risk management frameworks.
63. The monitoring and evaluation section of the funding proposal contains the required
information and is aligned with the relevant GCF policies and guidelines.

Independent Technical Advisory Panel’s assessment of
FP124
Proposal name: Strengthening Climate Resilience of Subsistence Farmers and
Agricultural Plantation Communities residing in the vulnerable
river basins, watershed areas and downstream of the Knuckles
Mountain Range Catchment of Sri Lanka
Accredited entity: International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)
Project/programme size: Small
I. Assessment of the independent Technical Advisory Panel
1.1 Impact potential Scale: Medium
1. The funding proposal is a small-scale project with a lifespan of six years that was
developed and submitted to GCF for financial support by the Government of Sri Lanka together
with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the accredited entity (AE). A
USD 39.78 million grant has been requested by the country from GCF for climate change
adaptation activities, and to leverage USD 9.2 million in co-financing (18.8 per cent of the total
project cost) from the Government of Sri Lanka.
2. This is the second submission from the AE elaborated based on the findings identified
by the independent Technical Advisory Panel (TAP) in a previous submission. The revised
funding proposal and additional annexes (annexes: 16(a) – project site climate analysis focused
on rainfall deficit; 16(b) – project site climate analysis focused on the trends of potential
evapotranspiration and moisture index; and 17 – hydrologic and climate analysis) are provided
in this submission. Improvements made are highlighted throughout the report.
3. The proposal targets ecosystems (biodiversity and water resources) in the
Knuckles/Amban Ganga highlands (upstream catchment) and lowlands (downstream
catchment). According to the information provided in the funding proposal, the Knuckles region
features mountains, valleys and a variety of ecosystems and species. Its importance is reflected
in the level of protection and international recognition that has been accorded at various times.
The Knuckles Conservation Forest,1 together with the Peak Wilderness Protected Area and
Horton Plains National Park (collectively referred to as the Central Highlands of Sri Lanka) was
declared a United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization World Heritage Site
in 2010. Aside from its scenic beauty, the Knuckles region is a vital watershed in the Mahaweli2
drainage system. It constitutes 30 per cent of the watershed forest of the Mahaweli catchment, a
major source of water for the country’s agricultural sector. The funding proposal considers that
these features make the Knuckles Conservation Forest an ideal site to introduce the IUCN Green
Listing process.3
1 In 2000 the Knuckles area was declared a Conservation Forest by the Forest Department, and in 2007 its buffer
zone was declared an Environmental Protection Area under the National Environmental Act.
2 Mahaweli is the largest river in Sri Lanka; the newly commissioned Moragahakanda and Kaluganga reservoirs also
depend on the watershed of the Knuckles Conservation Forest.
3 IUCN Green Listing is a green growth programme/activity. It focuses on branding and promotion of the site’s
commitment to certified conservation against standards and with this certification contributes to monitoring the
conservation process.

=== PAGE 147 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 147
4. The feasibility study showed that two monsoon seasons determine the climate
seasonality of Sri Lanka (the monsoon and inter-monsoon seasons). Sri Lanka’s territory is
characterized by three climatic zones: “wet zone”, “dry zone” and “intermediate zone”.
According to the records of the Department of Meteorology, a shifting in the climatic regions has
been observed in the period from 1960 to 2010, making the downstream catchment of the
project area drier due to the expanding dry zone, and the wet zone becoming the intermediate
zone. This shifting of the climate zones will further aggravate the existing water deficit in the
area.
5. The feasibility study also showed that rainfall, temperature and wind are key climatic
parameters impacting the territory of Sri Lanka, particularly the agriculture and water sectors.
The people and economy of Sri Lanka are heavily dependent on water for irrigation, domestic
and industrial use, and electricity generation. Rainfall in the wet and intermediate climatic
zones of the country is collected in an intricate series of reservoirs and delivered to the dry zone
agricultural lands. The water collection and delivery system is threatened by reservoirs silting
up at alarming rates. One of the reasons for increasing siltation in water-collecting reservoirs is
increased soil erosion in upstream catchments, partly intensified by increased rainfall intensity
during the monsoon seasons.
6. As regards the causes of siltation, a concern was raised by the independent TAP during
the first submission. In particular, information about the potential share of climate change in
increasing the siltation of reservoirs versus ineffective and unsustainable maintenance of the
system was not provided in the funding proposal. This information is crucial in decision-making
on the potential impact of planned measures (e.g. to direct more effort and resources to land
management or recommend measures for effective management of the maintenance of
irrigation systems). Such information would have an impact on proper planning of the project
exit strategy and ensure the long-term sustainability of the results, relevantly increasing the
impact of the funding proposal.
7. In the new submission, the AE provided additional information on soil erosion causes
and results of hydrological modelling of the Amban Ganga basin (covering the project area) and
experience from the adjacent Upper Mahaweli area for which more data are available
(hydrologic analysis – annex 17). In its response, the AE highlights the difficulty of reliably
separating the share of sediment yield attributable to more erosive rainfall (driven by climate
change) as opposed to soil erodibility (influenced by land cover and human activities). As a
result of hydrological modelling the AE reported that sediment yield is 2.2 times more sensitive
to rainfall erosivity than erodibility, indicating that between 56 and 67 per cent of increased
sediment yield is attributable to climate change. The AE also concludes that because of the
spatial and temporal scale of the modelling possible with available data, it is not unreasonable
to categorize sediment yield as only becoming an actionable problem because of climate change.
8. The target activities of the funding proposal are: (1) land and water; (2) land
degradation (erosion, leading to sedimentation); and (3) lack of water resources (in particular
in the dry downstream catchment area). The funding proposal concept and its potential impact
are described in paragraph 73 of the funding proposal. In particular, the paragraph states:
(a) The project makes interventions in the upstream area to help people adapt to climate
change by managing their land and water more sustainably and profitably. This
improves livelihoods of people in the upstream catchment (200,331 female and 183,759
male) while also contributing through environmental protection of the catchment
(166,254 ha) to maintaining the irrigation water supply to the downstream area
(506,264 ha, 122,150 of which are irrigated rice), where the project intervenes with
advice on climate resilient agriculture to ensure that efficient use is made of the water in
downstream agriculture thereby benefiting the very climate vulnerable dry zone
population (489,684 female and 469,442 male). The project therefore has an overall
reach of 672,518 ha and 1,343,216 people.

=== PAGE 148 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 148
9. The independent TAP is of the opinion that concentrating most of the activities in an
upstream area might not be the most effective approach, taking into consideration that the
downstream part of the catchment is much drier and has higher exposure to climate change. In
its response to the independent TAP the AE has clarified that focus on the upstream catchment
and sedimentation problem is a priority area decided by the government because the country
has two other complimentary projects (United Nations Development Programme/GCF project
implemented through the Ministry of Mahaweli Development and Environment, and the World
Bank funded project of USD 125 million implemented through the Ministry of Agriculture, see
para. 69 of the funding proposal). Both projects contribute mainly to the downstream
catchment area, improving rice agronomy through more efficient use of irrigation water in rice
cultivation, improving the irrigation system itself and developing rural advisory services
capacity.
10. The funding proposal has three components, and each has six subactivities. For
increased transparency and clarity of the concept and intervention considered, the measures
planned in the funding proposal at the subactivity level are provided below:
(a) Component 1: climate-resilient sustainable management of land and water (44 per cent
of GCF financing):
(i) Subactivity 1.1.1: streamside protection and drainage management along roads.
There are 2,373 km of streams and canals and 1,766 km of all types of roads in
the upper catchment from which the project intervention segments will be
selected;
(ii) Subactivity 1.1.2: rehabilitation and establishment of village tanks, ponds and
irrigation networks. The output of this subactivity includes 32 abandoned village
tanks and 121 functional ponds and tanks within the upper catchment area
rehabilitated (de-siltation) and new tanks established, increasing the irrigation
water availability in both upstream and downstream catchments;
(iii) Subactivity 1.1.3: restoration of forest mosaic landscapes. This activity focuses
on the following: restoring degraded forests within protected areas and forest
fragments; regrowing forests in priority areas for the supply of ecosystem
services, especially watershed protection; and the planting of trees outside
forests for improved sustainability and livelihoods. A dense forest of 41,911 ha,
an open forest of 21,905 ha, and a scrubland (degraded grassland) of 62,204 ha
will be rehabilitated. The project interventions will also improve the canopy
structure of the vegetation in the upland areas, thus enhancing cloud
interception and increased rain capture;
(iv) Subactivity 1.2.1: development of resilient farming techniques to grow
appropriate climate adapted varieties and make efficient use of irrigation water
and fertilizer (maximizing use of organic inputs and recycling) as well as
employing integrated pest control based on real-time weather and pest
incidence data (connected to the information system developed in subactivity
3.1.2). The output of this subactivity is that the cropping index4 will increase in
both the upstream and downstream catchments from 0.8 to 1.7 (a paddy of
122,150 ha downstream and of 8,793 ha upstream);
(v) Subactivity 1.2.2: intensification of sustainable smallholder production in the
upstream catchment (home gardens, analog forests,5 spice gardens and annual

(v) Subactivity 2.2.2: setting up a PES intermediary body, as a part of the multi-

nationally determined contribution (NDC), Sri Lanka’s national adaptation plan,

(c) Component 3: institutional capacity strengthened (29 per cent of GCF financing):

(ii) Subactivity 3.1.2: development of a shared information system to support land-

(vi) Subactivity 3.2.3: development and production of simple-to-use guidelines,
manuals and tools for matching options to contexts and implementing

11. One of the risky areas identified in the first submission of the funding proposal by the
independent TAP is related to the immediate effect and long-term sustainability of the results
achieved through component 1 and its subactivities 1.1.1, 1.1.2 and 1.1.3. Two key results are
anticipated from these subactivities: an increase in the availability of irrigation water for
irrigation rice through rehabilitation of irrigation systems (cleaning silted reservoirs, building
6 The core 4 framework is the general scheme for implementing the options by context approach. The four steps
applied in this approach are: diagnosis, principles, local adaptation and scaling.
7 Grama Niladhari divisions are village-level units.

new reservoirs, improving management of roads and canals/streams), and an increase in the
rainwater capture and retention potential of upstream catchments through improvement of
land management and vegetation. Regarding assessment of the long-term reliability and
sustainability of the results of these activities, the proposal did not provide data to suggest a
positive water balance in future.
12. In a new submission the updated climate analysis (annex 16(b)) was provided by the
AE. This analysis includes assessment of moisture index trend by 2050, which shows that, while
the dry zone project area will get drier in the key crop growing months of January and May
(creating a median requirement for 104.48 million cubic meters of irrigation water),
corresponding increases in the moisture index in the upstream project area from August to
October (median increase in surplus water of 237.61 million cubic meters) could potentially
compensate an increase in irrigation requirements if rainfall intensity on sedimentation is
reduced and storage reservoirs and water transfer channels are more protected from the
impact of sedimentation, which is one of the focus area of the funding proposal along with an
increase in rainwater collection capacity of the ecosystem.
13. The new submission provides a much detailed, area-specific feasibility study on changes
in climatic parameters driving the targeted sectors, but the results for assessment of water
supply and demand trends, taking climate change into consideration (and including the
approach for prioritization of consumers during decision-making) is not still provided.
14. It is the opinion of the independent TAP that the funding proposal could have high
impact on increasing the irrigation water supply in the downstream catchment, and ensure
sustainable land management in upstream catchment in the Knuckles region of Sri Lanka.
However, taking into consideration the ambitious plans of the Government of Sri Lanka to
expand the irrigated paddy area, sustainability of the impact will be limited in future. At this
stage of the assessment a demonstration of sustainable management of the water supply
process is not provided, but it will be implemented as a condition to approval of the funding
proposal. This capacity gap in long-term sustainable management of the water supply and
demand process makes the impact score “medium”.
1.2 Paradigm shift potential Scale: High
15. The funding proposal aims at implementation of several transformational elements:
(a) Component 2 (subactivities 2.2.1, 2.2.2 and 2.2.3) of the funding proposal supports
establishment of a PES mechanism. Three potential income streams have already been
identified in the funding proposal: a levy on hydropower generation; a levy on export
crops used to incentivize best practices in plantations; and the use of general taxation
receipts to incentivize smallholder farmers to adopt sustainable land-use practices,
building on the existing system of welfare payments. The Government of Sri Lanka has
already committed in the project proposal to implement the hydropower levy as a PES
mechanism. There is already a levy on export crops that pays for support services to the
sector, and the project plans to explore possibilities to extend this to support catchment
management together with other options for channelling some of the increased income
envisioned from value chain upgrading under output 2.1 in both the plantation sector
and amongst smallholder farmers to develop novel sustainable PES modalities from
increased revenue associated with sustainable production;
(b) One of the subactivities (2.1.2) enables the policy environment for use of Green Listing
(for nature, culture and heritage elements) to enhance community income and engage
the climate-affected vulnerable poor. Currently the beneficiaries are not engaged in the
development of various social welfare schemes created to support the vulnerable. This
subactivity aims to leverage government investments in subsidies and make it

=== PAGE 152 ===
GCF/B.25/02/Add.01
Page 152
compulsory for beneficiaries and vulnerable groups to be part of the green activities that
generate income for them while supporting conservation. Connecting these groups with
a PES mechanism would be more meaningful and sustainable in order to minimize
subsidies. In addition, the project will provide the Green List label to local tourism
providers, local stakeholders such as non-governmental or civil society organizations
directly supporting the protected area to achieve successful conservation outcomes.
This process should contribute to equitably sharing collected tourism benefits more
centrally;
(c) One more transformational element considered in the funding proposal is
implementation of sustainable land management practices, mainly in the upstream
catchment area, which will improve the climate change adaptive capacity of biodiversity,
agriculture and irrigation systems; and
(d) For strengthening the national and regional capacities in climate resilient, sustainable
management of the vulnerable river basins in watershed areas and downstream of the
Knuckles Mountain Range catchment area of Sri Lanka the funding proposal plans to put
in operation decision-making supporting tools for data collection and analysis. Tools
required for climate pressure and water deficit analysis should include, as minimum,
tools for assessment of trends of potential evapotranspiration, crop-related water
deficit, moisture index, soil-water hydrology, water supply-demand (e.g. WEAP8
software or any other similar tool available) and others.
16. In conclusion, the paradigm shift is assessed as “high” subject to successful
implementation of conditions provided in section II. Despite the local nature of adaptation
measures, the knowledge system and capacity established by the funding proposal for
sustainable planning of land use and water resources in the Knuckles region could be replicated
in other regions of Sri Lanka as well as at national level.
1.3 Sustainable development potential Scale: High
17. Sri Lanka’s national adaptation plan identifies various adaptation options and
performance indicators for the nine identified most vulnerable sectors. This funding proposal
directly addresses four of the nine vulnerable sectors: food security, water resources,
ecosystems and biodiversity, and export development all of which contribute to sustainable
development processes.
18. Component 2 of the funding proposal aims to establish a PES mechanism to transfer
value realized from using water derived from the upstream catchment to fund catchment
protection. As mentioned in the “paradigm shift” investment criterion section, three potential
income streams have already been identified in the funding proposal, a levy on hydropower
generation, a levy on export crops used to incentivize best practices in plantations and the use
of general taxation receipts to incentivize smallholder farmers to adopt sustainable land-use
practices, building on the existing system of welfare payments. In case of successful
implementation of these mechanisms they could significantly contribute to the sustainable
management of ecosystems and strengthen ecosystem services.
19. The funding proposal will contribute to several SDGs and their target areas:
(a) SDG 15, “life on land”. The highest contribution would probably be to this SDG, which is
focused on forests, desertification and biodiversity. One of the target areas of this SDG is
to ensure the conservation of mountain ecosystems, including their biodiversity, to
8 “Water Evaluation and Planning” system is a user-friendly software tool that takes an integrated approach to water
resources planning.
